topics: Atomic number, mass, shells and quantum numbers
Orbital filling and the periodic table
Space lattice, unit cell and crystal systems
BCC, FCC and HCP: numbers, APF and lattice-parameter relations
Surface defects, eutectic freezing and single crystals
Constitutional supercooling and special solidification processes
Strain energy, dissociation and stacking faults
Climb, cross-slip, interactions, Frank–Read sources and pile-ups
Grain refinement and the Hall–Petch relationship
Fick's second law and the error-function solution

learningObjectives.description: Explain the scope of physical metallurgy and the composition–processing–microstructure–properties relationship.
Distinguish atomic number, mass number, proton count and neutron count.
Determine maximum electron capacities of shells, subshells and orbitals.
Interpret principal, azimuthal, magnetic and spin quantum numbers.
Apply the Pauli exclusion principle to electron occupancy.
Classify elements as metals, metalloids and non-metals using periodic-table position and characteristics.
Apply orbital-filling order and electron-configuration rules.
Relate transition-metal electron configurations to variable valence and chemical behaviour.
Explain ionic, covalent, metallic and secondary bonding mechanisms.
Compare primary and secondary bonds by strength, directionality and physical origin.
Relate bond type and directionality to conductivity, ductility, brittleness and cohesion.
Identify bonding within and between the layers of graphite and in diamond's covalent network.
Explain dipole interactions and hydrogen bonding as secondary bonding.
Identify equilibrium interatomic spacing from the minimum of a potential-energy curve.
Relate potential-well depth and curvature to cohesive energy, melting temperature and elastic modulus.
Explain thermal expansion through anharmonicity and asymmetry of the interatomic potential.
Distinguish the individual attractive and repulsive forces from their zero resultant at equilibrium.
Interpret the attractive and repulsive terms in a mathematical interatomic potential and the condition for short-range repulsion.
Explain the space-lattice concept and identify the role of a unit cell in generating a crystal.
Interpret lattice parameters, crystal-system constraints and the three-dimensional Bravais-lattice classification.
Compare BCC, FCC and HCP by atoms per unit cell, coordination number and atomic packing factor.
Derive contact directions and lattice-parameter–atomic-radius relationships for BCC and FCC.
Identify BCC, FCC and HCP structures, their close-packed stacking sequences and their implications for packing.
Use the ideal HCP axial ratio and interpret deviations in real HCP metals.
Use standard crystallographic notation for directions, direction families, planes and plane families.
Determine Miller indices from plane intercepts, including parallel and negative intercepts.
Calculate interplanar spacing for cubic crystals and relate it to lattice parameter and atomic radius.
Relate close-packed planes and directions, equivalent plane families and available slip systems to deformation behaviour.
Define and calculate linear and planar atomic density.
Locate octahedral and tetrahedral interstitial sites and compare their number and relative size in common crystal structures.
Explain interstitial carbon accommodation, local lattice strain and carbon solubility in ferrite and austenite.
Relate supersaturated interstitial carbon to martensite tetragonality.
Describe the sequence and crystal structures of iron allotropes.
Explain the FCC-to-BCC transformation in iron, carbon-solubility changes and martensite formation by quenching.
Apply Bragg's law to calculate X-ray diffraction angles from wavelength and interplanar spacing.
Explain the geometric origin of the path difference in Bragg diffraction.
